Subject: Discovery follow-up: performance constraints & routing playbook

Hi Daniel — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and a set of concrete asks so we can move toward a scoped POC: 

TL;DR: OpsGenix needs sub-250ms p95 for 1–2 concurrent real-time assistant sessions per user (streaming responses), target throughput ~150 req/s at peak, and input+output combined token ceiling ~12k tokens. Raised concerns about spikes and burst behavior during heavy document ingestion.

Key points we captured: 
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 250ms for user-facing streaming completions (note: p50 target is ~80ms).
- Throughput: baseline 40 req/s, peak 150 req/s for 30-minute windows.
- Concurrency: expect up to 600 concurrent long-lived websocket streams across their EU+US footprint (most traffic US).
- Streaming requirements: incremental token delivery (chunked) with <= 100ms flush for small chunks.
- Context window: typical request will include a 9k-token document + 1k token user prompt; outputs vary but budget ~2k tokens output. They explicitly called out the need to support ~12k total context in some flows.
- Fault model: when overloaded, OpsGenix prefers graceful degradation (shorter outputs / switch to smaller model) rather than hard failures. They asked about routing policies and circuit-breaker options.

Asks / next steps for Redwood: 
1) Can the hosted endpoint meet p95 <= 250ms for streaming with a 12k token context in our dedicated config? Call out model variant + quantization assumptions.
2) Proposed routing playbook: which models we recommend for normal vs degraded modes; what auto-fallback latencies look like.
3) Suggested circuit-breaker thresholds (concurrency/queue size) and recommended hedging/backpressure behavior.
4) An initial perf matrix (server-side token breakdown + expected latency per token segment) we can share in the proposal.

I’ve CC’d Aditya and Marissa to help with the technical details and numbers. Daniel — if I missed anything or the token ceilings are off, please flag. If okay, we’ll follow up with a short perf plan and a draft mutual action plan.

Thanks,
Naomi

Thanks Naomi — that's accurate and very helpful. Couple clarifications: 

- The 12k token ceiling is our upper bound for legal-doc ingestion flows; 90% of flows are <= 6k tokens.
- For streaming UX we need token chunks to arrive visibly within ~150ms for the first chunk, then ~100ms thereafter for small subsequences.
- Regional split: ~75% US, ~25% EU. If routing to EU introduces a >40ms region penalty that's acceptable, but we can't tolerate >100ms cross-region added latency.

We are happy to run a small POC (2 weeks) if you can provide a validated perf matrix and a model routing playbook. Also, procurement will need expected request/unit pricing for peak and degraded modes; I loop them in on next note.

—Daniel

Hi all — draft numbers and operational playbook below. I attached a perf_matrix.xlsx stub with measured microbenchmarks (single-token decode timings extrapolated to streaming chunk sizes) and memory estimates. Attachment: perf_matrix.xlsx.

Summary (short):
- Models tested: rdx-7b-int8 (baseline low-latency), rdx-13b-q4 (higher quality), rdx-13b-slim (quantized variant for degraded mode).
- Hosted vs Dedicated: Dedicated GPU pools (single-tenant) required to guarantee p95 <= 250ms at 12k context for streaming at ~40 req/s. For their peak 150 req/s we recommend a dedicated autoscale cluster with reserved capacity + burst buffer. Hosted shared endpoints will hit queueing and/or degrade QoS for 12k contexts at peak.

Perf bullets (streaming path, measured on A100-like infra):
- 3k total tokens (rdx-7b-int8): p50 60ms, p95 120ms.
- 6k total tokens (rdx-7b-int8): p50 95ms, p95 180ms.
- 12k total tokens (rdx-13b-q4, streaming): p50 160ms, p95 260–300ms (single-instance numbers; multi-instance and dedicated routing bring p95 closer to ~240ms with prefix caching + KV reuse).

Notes on what influences latency: longer input context increases KV cache population time and attention kernel cost roughly superlinearly; streaming amortizes decode costs but initial token latency is dominated by attention prep. Prefix/KV caching for repeated document slices reduces subsequent request latency by up to 40%.

Routing playbook (recommendation):
- Normal: rdx-13b-q4 in Dedicated cluster for legal doc flows >8k tokens. Use prefix caching for repeated sections.
- Degraded (policy 1 - latency pressure): switch to rdx-13b-slim (smaller quantized variant) when queue length > 8 or average model latency > 220ms for 30s sliding window. This preserves quality but reduces latency by ~15–25%.
- Emergency (policy 2 - capacity exhausted): switch to rdx-7b-int8 and shorten outputs (configurable output token cap) when queue length > 20 or sustained CPU/GPU oversubscription detected. Emit an advisory event to the client to indicate degraded quality.

Circuit-breaker thresholds (starting suggestion):
- Concurrency per model shard: 12 active streams per GPU (tunable).
- Request queue cap: 200 requests across the cluster; beyond that, start shedding with 503 + de-elevated routed fallback.
- Sliding-window latency trigger: p95 > 240ms for 60s => trigger policy 1.

Canary/POC plan (2-week):
Week 1: Dedicated small cluster (3 GPUs) — run synthetic mix with: 70% <=6k flows, 20% 8k flows, 10% 12k flows. Measure p50/p95 and streaming flush timings.
Week 2: Scale to target (simulate 150 req/s peak) with Autoscale and validate failover rules, circuit-breakers, and observed degradation modes.

Pricing note for procurement: we will prepare a tiered estimate: baseline (normal ops), degraded-mode surcharge (per-token uplift when fallback engaged), and reserved-capacity commitment options. I can draft numbers once commercial confirms target commit tier.

Attachments: perf_matrix.xlsx (microbenchmark sheet), redwood-routing-playbook.pdf (operational playbook draft).

Let me know if you want me to join the next call with OpsGenix to walk the perf matrix and the canary steps.
